title: Shared Sea Atlas
concept: A wall of paired maps connects the Seto Inland Sea to the larger systems that pass through it. Each world map has a Japan companion. Visitors move between the two scales, then leave a question on a paper table.
reason: Awashima’s shipping history gives the work a local starting point. The Maritime Memorial Hall or another agreed indoor room is a candidate, not a booked venue. The work asks residents which routes and materials deserve attention.
experience: Start with Earth and Water. Find Japan without placing it at the centre of the world.
Compare six world/Japan pairs: land, water, cables, atmosphere, refinery throughput and temperature.
At a seated table, add an anonymous question or draw a route that matters to island life. Visitors may take their contribution home.
footprint: One indoor room, approximately 6 × 8 m; at least 8 m of usable wall; six paired panels and one 1.8 × 0.8 m table.
materials: Twelve pigment prints, each 1,117.6 × 483.9 mm; reusable hanging rails; printed Japanese/English labels; paper and pencils. No network connection is needed.
review: Confirm the room, wall loads, clear routes and host capacity. Ask island partners to select the local questions and agree how contributions will be kept or returned.

title: The Port and the Cloud
site: Uno or Takamatsu / an indoor port-side room
concept: Four map pairs show the physical systems behind a familiar word: cloud. Cables, data centres, ground stations and atmospheric clouds sit beside one another. A reading table makes their different meanings clear.
reason: A port already connects visible movement with distant infrastructure. The display uses that experience without suggesting that a cable line proves a local landing or that a data-centre point measures electricity use.
experience: Follow one cable route across the world plate.
Compare it with the groundstation and cloud/CDN inventories, keeping their dates visible.
Read the atmosphere plate as weather observations with distinct acquisition dates. Write one question about what remains unseen.
footprint: Indoor room around 5 × 6 m; four paired wall panels; one low reading table; seated alternative to every wall text.
materials: Eight full-size prints; freestanding reusable panels; a source booklet; paper question cards. Optional recorded conversation only after speaker agreement.
review: Confirm a host room outside ferry circulation. Review infrastructure captions for unsupported claims. Obtain speaker and recording agreements before producing audio.

title: Heat, Salt, Water
site: Utazu / near the town’s salt-making history
concept: A small atlas puts land temperature, water, food, fisheries and oil refining beside one another. The installation invites comparison of systems while making their different units and time periods visible.
reason: Utazu’s salt-making history offers a concrete entry into energy, evaporation and labour. Residents can correct the exhibition’s questions before the final labels are printed.
experience: Begin with the water plate and a short account of the host’s chosen local history.
Read the temperature map as record-day counts, not as a forecast of island weather.
Compare food and fisheries statistics with refinery throughput. A caption explains what each measure can and cannot say about the islands.
footprint: Indoor room around 6 × 6 m; five paired panels; one reading table; no process equipment or water installation.
materials: Ten full-size prints; modular rails; source cards; tactile sample of folded paper. No extraction, salt production demonstration or environmental sensing is proposed.
review: Agree the local historical account and credit contributors. Have a reader check that national statistics are not presented as measurements of Utazu.

title: Fold a World, Read an Island
site: Shido or Takamatsu / an accessible workshop room
concept: Participants cut, fold and annotate a paper world map. A world/Japan comparison becomes a practical lesson in how a map changes attention. Each person chooses whether to keep or share their sheet.
reason: The supplied conference ideas include a rip, burn, fold workshop. This proposal develops the paper-folding part into a low-equipment public session; it uses no burning.
experience: A ten-minute demonstration compares globe, flat map and Japan detail.
In pairs, fold an A3 study sheet and mark a route, material or question.
A closing table conversation lets participants explain their choices; no personal location data is collected.
footprint: Two 90-minute sessions, up to 20 people each; a 6 × 6 m accessible room; five worktables and a seated demonstration.
materials: A3 study prints, blunt scissors, pencils, reusable templates and large-print instructions. Full-size masters remain available as wall references.
review: Confirm the host, participant age range and access needs. Review translations and provide a no-cut alternative. Photography requires separate participant agreement.

title: What Does the Cloud Touch?
concept: A moderated conversation connects digital networks to cables, ports, energy and everyday work. Three map pairs anchor the discussion. The audience leaves with a short source guide.
reason: The conference memo names cloud/network and media themes. Nicole Starosielski, Jennifer Holt, Lisa Nakamura and Eric Rodenbeck are possible invitation leads, not confirmed contributors.
experience: A short map reading establishes what the sources measure.
Two invited contributors and a local respondent discuss one concrete route or material dependency.
Audience questions are followed by a facilitated source-table conversation, with an option to contribute in writing.
footprint: One 90-minute conversation for about 50 visitors; accessible indoor seating; three paired maps and a source table.
materials: Six reference prints, microphones if the room requires them, bilingual handout and live interpretation allowance. No recording is assumed.
review: Secure contributors, define a topic with the local respondent, and confirm interpretation. International travel beyond the allowance would require a revised budget or remote participation.

title: An Island Seen from Two Scales
concept: A short guided walk alternates between looking at the island and reading maps. Participants record observations in words or sketches. The activity ends at a seated table so walking is optional.
reason: Megijima’s shore, wind walls and settlement offer places to discuss what a global map leaves out. A resident host selects the route and the subjects; this is not a survey of residents.
experience: Meet indoors and choose a walking or seated version.
Visit three agreed stopping places over 45 minutes. Compare observed surroundings with dated map layers.
Return for a 30-minute table discussion. Keep sketches with their makers unless they explicitly choose to contribute them.
footprint: Two sessions of up to 12 people; route under 1 km if approved; an indoor alternative for weather or access.
materials: A4 study sheets, clipboards, pencils and a large seated map. No tracking app, drone or collection of identifiable location histories.
review: Walk the route with the host; confirm step-free alternatives, tide/weather decisions and a cancellation contact. Keep visitor routes clear of working areas.

title: The Port Reading Table
site: Uno / an agreed indoor waiting or community space
concept: A durable table holds a sequence of world and Japan map sheets. A traveller can read one sheet in a minute or stay with the whole atlas. The table operates without a screen or network.
reason: The format meets the variable time of a port visit. It must sit in a host-controlled room with free circulation, not in a boarding queue or an emergency route.
experience: Choose a tab: water, cables, energy or heat.
Turn a world sheet to its Japan companion.
Read the date and one clear limitation; take a small printed guide if wanted.
footprint: About 3 × 3 m including circulation; one 1.8 × 0.8 m table with seated reach and knee clearance; eight A2 study sheets.
materials: Reusable timber or metal table, replaceable protected paper sheets, tabbed bindings and printed guide. Full print masters supply the source artwork.
review: Confirm dimensions with access users and host staff; approve cleaning, sheet replacement and storage. Test glare and reading distance on a physical sample.

title: Maps in the Wind’s Shelter
site: Ogijima / a sheltered, non-heritage courtyard candidate
season: One 2028 season, subject to exposure review
concept: Three reversible fabric panels place world maps on one face and Japan details on the other. Visitors turn a panel by hand within a sheltered structure. The work makes scale a physical choice.
reason: Ogijima’s dense settlement and wind-protection practices inform the idea. The structure must be designed for the actual site and must not attach to historic walls.
experience: Approach three panels at walking speed.
Turn one panel to compare world and Japan views.
Read a short seated copy of each label and return the panel to its resting position.
footprint: Indicative 4 × 4 m footprint; three 1.2 × 0.65 m panels; maximum proposed height 1.8 m. Dimensions are design assumptions pending site and engineering review.
materials: Printed fabric, rounded reusable frames, controlled hinges and an engineered support. No ground anchoring or historic-wall fixing is assumed.
review: Required before fabrication: site permission, structural review, wind and weather operating limits, pinch-point review and an indoor fallback. This is the most complex option.

title: The Island Atlas Desk
site: Ibukijima / a former-school or community-room candidate
concept: An ordinary desk becomes a compact atlas of sea, food, energy and sky. Fold-out sheets and a source book let visitors read at their own pace. A host can change the sequence during the season.
reason: The supplied site report connects Ibukijima with iriko production and a former school. A desk respects the scale of a room and leaves room for a locally chosen account of work and sea.
experience: Open a labelled drawer or folder.
Unfold one world sheet beside its Japan companion.
Read a short local text commissioned with the host, then return the sheet for the next visitor.
footprint: About 3 × 3 m; one adapted 1.6 × 0.8 m desk, two chairs and a wall reference. No power or internet is needed.
materials: Repairable desk, four pairs of folded A2 sheets, large-print source book and replaceable folders. Celestial sheets are clearly labelled as Setouchi observer views.
review: Agree room use, desk access and local text ownership. Test folding durability and give the host spare copies and a clear replacement method.
